::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you do three experiments on the computer and
record what you see. Do each experiment when your teacher shows it. After
each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy your key results
into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with Excel, a browser, your university
  account, and your phone (its stopwatch).
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the three experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. On the
  interactive lesson, every step has "Check your result". Look only after
  you try.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · By hand or with AutoSum?

**Aim:** measure how much time an app saves on a simple, repeated job.
*(Lesson notes 1.1 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Open `prices-start.xlsx`. Start the stopwatch on your phone. Add the
   eight prices in A2:A9 in your head or on paper. Stop the watch.

   {{< record "My total … JD ; my time … seconds" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The total is **150 JD** (10 + 25 + 15 + 30 + 20 + 5 + 35 + 10). By hand,
   most students need 20 to 40 seconds, and some make a mistake.
   :::

2. Click A10. On the Home tab, click **AutoSum** (Σ), then press Enter.

   {{< record "A10 shows … ; its formula is …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **150** with **=SUM(A2:A9)**, in about 2 seconds.
   :::

3. Change the price in A4 from 15 to **25**. Look at A10.

   {{< record "A10 now shows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **160**, at once. By hand you must add all the prices again; the
   spreadsheet does it by itself. This is productivity: more useful work in
   less time.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · The apps of Microsoft 365

**Aim:** find the main productivity apps and the job of each one.
*(Lesson notes 1.2 · about 12 minutes)*

1. Press the Windows key and type **Excel**. Do the same for **Word** and
   **PowerPoint**. Which of the three can you find?

   {{< record "I found" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   All three: Word, Excel and PowerPoint are installed on the lab computers.
   If one is missing, use it in the browser at `office.com`.
   :::

2. In the browser, open `office.com` and sign in with your university
   account. Write the names of four apps that you see.

   {{< record "Four apps" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: four of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, OneDrive and
   Teams (the list can also show Forms or OneNote).
   :::

3. Which app is right for each job: a CV, a chart of the sales, slides for a
   talk, your files on every device?

   {{< record "CV … ; chart … ; slides … ; files …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Word** (a word processor), **Excel** (a spreadsheet), **PowerPoint** (a
   presentation app), **OneDrive** (cloud storage).
   :::

## Experiment 3 · A first prompt

**Aim:** ask an AI assistant in normal words, and check its answer.
*(Lesson notes 1.3 · about 14 minutes)*

1. Open an AI assistant that the university allows, for example
   `copilot.microsoft.com` with your university account. Type this prompt:
   *Write 3 short tips for a polite e-mail to a teacher.*

   {{< record "The first tip, in a few words" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: three short tips, for example "Start with a greeting",
   "Say why you write" and "Thank the teacher at the end". Your words may
   differ: the AI writes a new text for every person.
   :::

2. Start a new chat and type the same prompt again. Is the answer the same?

   {{< record "Same answer or a new one?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **A new one**: the tips are similar, but the words change. The AI makes
   new text each time, so you read every answer before you use it.
   :::

3. Ask: *When did Sunrise Company open its first shop?*

   {{< record "What the AI says" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Sunrise Company is a made-up company of this course, so no answer can be
   true. A good AI says that it does not know. If it gives a date, the date
   is invented: AI can sound sure and still be wrong. Check facts in a real
   source.
   :::

4. Copy the three tips into Word. Change one tip into your own words and
   make it **bold**. Save the file as **tips.docx**.

   {{< record "The tip in my words" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good answer: one tip in your words, for example "Write the course name
   in the subject line", in bold, in `tips.docx`. You read every tip before
   you used it.
   :::
